lead: A Bayesian belief network (Bayes net) is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are random variables. Each node stores a conditional probability table for itself given its parents. The graph gives a compact way to write one large joint probability as a product of small local factors. It is used in diagnosis, fault finding, risk analysis and spam filtering, where causes and effects are linked and evidence arrives piece by piece. This chapter shows the product rule, the independence the graph encodes, and inference by enumeration and variable elimination.
prereq: You need 3.2 Bayes theorem and conditional probability from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A Bayesian belief network is a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a random variable X<sub>i</sub>. An arrow points from a parent to a child and says the parent directly affects the child. Acyclic means no directed loop: following arrows never returns to the same node.

Each node stores a conditional probability table (CPT). The CPT gives P(X<sub>i</sub> | parents(X<sub>i</sub>)) for every parent combination. A root node has no parents, so its table is P(X<sub>i</sub>).

blocks.where: P(X1,…,Xn) is the joint probability of one full assignment; parents(Xi) is the set of parent values of node i; the product runs over all n nodes.

blocks.text: The product is compact. A full joint table for n binary variables needs 2ⁿ − 1 numbers. A Bayes net with at most k parents per node needs about n·2ᵏ numbers. This saving is why the graph exists.
For the fear–study–pass chain, P(F)=0.3. The Study CPT has P(S|F)=0.8 and P(S|¬F)=0.5. The Pass CPT has P(P|S)=0.9 and P(P|¬S)=0.3. One joint entry is P(F=true, S=true, P=true)=0.3×0.8×0.9=0.216.

Conditional independence means X and Y are independent given Z when P(X,Y|Z)=P(X|Z)P(Y|Z). A Bayes net encodes a local rule: each node is independent of its non-descendants given its parents. This is the Markov condition.

In the chain Fear → Study → Pass, Study blocks the path. Given Study, Fear and Pass are independent: P(Pass | Study, Fear)=P(Pass | Study). Without conditioning on Study, Fear and Pass are dependent. The arrow directions give the factorization; they need not prove causation.
To build a Bayes net from a problem description:

items: List the random variables and their possible values.
Add an arrow from each direct parent to its child.
Check that no directed cycle exists.
Write one CPT for each node from its parents.
Read the joint as the product of all CPTs.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this a Bayes net or belief network.
Inference computes a query probability from the joint, given evidence. Evidence fixes some variables. Hidden variables are summed out. With query Q and evidence E=e:
P(Q | E=e) = α Σ<sub>h</sub> P(Q, E=e, h)
blocks.where: α=1/P(E=e) normalises the result; h ranges over all assignments of the hidden variables; P(Q,E=e,h) is read from the joint product.

blocks.text: Enumeration repeats many sums. Variable elimination pushes each sum inward. A factor is a table over a set of variables. Multiply all factors that contain the hidden variable, then sum that variable out. The order matters: a good order keeps intermediate factors small.

items: Write the joint as a product of CPT factors.
Fix every evidence variable to its observed value.
Pick a hidden variable, multiply its factors, sum it out, and keep the new factor.
Repeat until only query and evidence variables remain.
Multiply the remaining factors and divide by P(E=e).

blocks.text: For P(Pass) in the chain, eliminate Fear first: Σ<sub>F</sub> P(F)P(S|F) gives P(S). Then eliminate Study: Σ<sub>S</sub> P(S)P(Pass|S) gives P(Pass). The next example computes both values.

figure.caption: Fear influences Study, and Study influences Pass. Each node carries a table for itself given its parents, so the joint is P(F)P(S|F)P(P|S).

spec.aria: A Bayesian belief network Fear to Study to Pass, with a conditional probability table stored on each node.

examples.question: Fear F has P(F)=0.3. Study S has P(S|F)=0.8 and P(S|¬F)=0.5. Pass P has P(P|S)=0.9 and P(P|¬S)=0.3. Use variable elimination with order F, then S to find P(Pass). Give every factor and intermediate value.
steps: Write the query: P(P)=Σ<sub>S</sub> Σ<sub>F</sub> P(F)P(S|F)P(P|S).
Eliminate F. For S=true: f(S=true)=0.3×0.8 + 0.7×0.5 = 0.24 + 0.35 = 0.59. This is P(S=true).
Eliminate S for the query P=true: P(P=true)=0.9×0.59 + 0.3×0.41 = 0.531 + 0.123 = 0.654.
examples.check:
pF = 0.3
pS_given_F = 0.8
pS_given_notF = 0.5
pP_given_S = 0.9
pP_given_notS = 0.3
pS_true = pS_given_F * pF + pS_given_notF * (1 - pF)
pS_false = 1 - pS_true
pP_true = pP_given_S * pS_true + pP_given_notS * pS_false
pP_false = 1 - pP_true
print(pS_true)
print(pS_false)
print(pP_true)
print(pP_false)

traps: A CPT is P(child | parents), not P(parents | child). Writing P(F|S) where the table needs P(S|F) reverses the query.
Do not create a directed cycle. A cycle makes the product rule meaningless because no node can be first.
P(Pass) needs a sum over Study. Using only P(Pass|S)=0.9 gives a conditional probability, not the marginal.
In the chain, Fear and Pass are dependent overall. They become independent only when Study is observed.
With evidence, normalise by P(E=e). Do not divide by 1 or by the number of hidden states.

quiz.q: What does DAG mean, and why must a Bayesian belief network be acyclic?
quiz.a: DAG means directed acyclic graph. A directed cycle would make the joint product rule invalid because no node could be first.

quiz.q: Why can a Bayes net store fewer numbers than a full joint table?
quiz.a: The joint factorises into local CPTs. Each node depends only on its parents, so only the parent combinations are stored, not every full assignment.

quiz.q: Fear F has P(F)=0.4. Study S has P(S|F)=0.7 and P(S|¬F)=0.2. Find P(S).
Use the chapter values P(S)=0.59, P(P|S)=0.9 and P(P|¬S)=0.3. Find P(P=true, S=true).
In Fear → Study → Pass, are Fear and Pass independent given Study? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: Yes. Study blocks the chain, so P(Pass | Study, Fear)=P(Pass | Study).

quiz.q: A modeller adds an edge Pass → Study to Fear → Study → Pass. Why is this invalid?
quiz.a: It creates the directed cycle Study → Pass → Study. The graph is no longer a DAG, so the product factorisation fails.

quiz.q: Write the joint for the graph A → B, A → C, B → C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial systems use approximate inference such as loopy belief propagation, MCMC and variational methods when exact sums are too large. Libraries include pgmpy in Python and bnlearn in R. The same graph ideas appear in causal inference, fault diagnosis and risk models. Search for "Bayesian network variable elimination" and "d-separation".
